title: Marginal-constrained Entropy Accumulation Theorem
authors: Amir Arqand And Ernest Y.-Z. Tan
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2273 (2026).

We derive a novel chain rule for a family of channel conditional entropies, covering von Neumann and sandwiched Rényi entropies. In the process, we show that these channel conditional entropies are equal to their regularized version, and more generally, additive across tensor products of channels. For the purposes of cryptography, applying our chain rule to sequences of channels yields a new variant of Rényi entropy accumulation, in which we can impose some specific forms of marginal-state constraint on the input states to each individual channel. This generalizes a recently introduced security proof technique that was developed to analyze prepare-and-measure QKD with no limitations on the repetition rate. In particular, our generalization yields “fully adaptive'' protocols that can in principle update the entropy estimation procedure during the protocol itself, similar to the quantum probability estimation framework.

.
tldr: The paper proves a marginal-constrained entropy accumulation theorem via a new chain rule for channel conditional entropies, enabling fully adaptive security proofs for prepare-and-measure QKD.
motivation: Entropy accumulation is central to composable security proofs in quantum cryptography, but existing variants have limitations on input-state constraints and protocol adaptivity.
method: The authors derive a chain rule for a family of channel conditional entropies covering von Neumann and sandwiched Rényi entropies, show equality with their regularized versions, and apply this to sequences of channels to obtain a new Rényi entropy accumulation theorem with marginal-state constraints.
result: The resulting marginal-constrained EAT generalizes a recent security-proof technique for prepare-and-measure QKD without repetition-rate limitations and supports fully adaptive protocols that can update entropy estimation during the protocol.
conclusion: This work strengthens the entropy accumulation toolkit for quantum cryptography by relaxing constraints and enabling adaptive security analyses, with direct implications for QKD security proofs.

title: Geometric Characterization Of non-Gaussian Entanglement For Finite Stellar Rank States
authors: Carlos E. Lopetegui-Gonzalez, Massimo Frigerio, And Mattia Walschaers
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2269 (2026).

We introduce a general framework for the analysis of non-Gaussian entanglement in bosonic states of finite stellar rank. The central result is the full characterization of their entanglement structure through the atomic decomposition of their stellar polynomial and its associated structural graph, whose connected components determine the mode-intrinsic entanglement content of the state and all partitions compatible with passive separability. An essential ingredient in this construction is the concept of essential variables, which identify the minimal number of effective modes involved in a core state, in direct correspondence with the symplectic rank. This reduction provides the foundation for decomposing stellar polynomials into atomic factors and for revealing the underlying entanglement structure. Building on this, we derive complete separability criteria for two-mode states, expressed through hyperplane decompositions of zero sets, and for stellar-rank-2 states across an arbitrary number of modes. Applications to several example states illustrate how the method isolates genuinely non-Gaussian resources and quantifies preparation complexity.

.
tldr: The paper develops a geometric framework for characterizing non-Gaussian entanglement in bosonic states with finite stellar rank using stellar polynomials, essential variables, and structural graphs.
motivation: Non-Gaussian entanglement in continuous-variable bosonic systems is a key resource but lacks a general structural characterization comparable to Gaussian entanglement theory.
method: The authors introduce atomic decompositions of stellar polynomials and associated structural graphs, define essential variables corresponding to symplectic rank, and derive separability criteria via hyperplane decompositions of zero sets.
result: They obtain complete separability criteria for two-mode states and for stellar-rank-2 states with arbitrary mode number, and show how connected components of the structural graph determine mode-intrinsic entanglement and passive-separability-compatible partitions.
conclusion: The framework isolates genuinely non-Gaussian entanglement resources and quantifies preparation complexity, providing a structural foundation for entanglement theory beyond Gaussian states.

title: Bounding The Entanglement Of A State From Its Spectrum
authors: Jofre Abellanet-Vidal, Guillem Müller-Rigat, Albert Rico, And Anna Sanpera
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2260 (2026).

We introduce a framework to upper bound the entanglement content of a bipartite quantum state from its spectrum alone. Using linear maps and their inverses, we derive rigorous constraints on the maximal entanglement that can be activated under global unitary transformations. We use as entanglement quantifiers the negativity and the Schmidt number; however, our framework is general and applies to any other entanglement measure. Our approach yields compact analytical sufficient criteria for bounding the entanglement of full-rank states in arbitrary dimensions and reveals new spectral constraints on Schmidt number witnesses.

.
tldr: The paper introduces a framework to upper bound bipartite entanglement from the spectrum alone using linear maps and their inverses, with applications to negativity and Schmidt number.
motivation: Entanglement quantification typically requires full state tomography, so bounding entanglement from spectral data alone is practically and theoretically valuable.
method: The authors use linear maps and inverse maps to derive rigorous spectral constraints on the maximal entanglement activatable under global unitary transformations, focusing on negativity and Schmidt number.
result: They obtain compact analytical sufficient criteria for bounding entanglement of full-rank states in arbitrary dimensions and find new spectral constraints on Schmidt number witnesses.
conclusion: The framework provides a general spectral approach to entanglement bounding that applies beyond negativity and Schmidt number and yields useful analytical criteria.

title: Post-selection Games
authors: Víctor Calleja Rodríguez, Ivan A. Bocanegra-Garay, And Mateus Araújo
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2259 (2026).

In this paper, we introduce post-selection games, a generalization of nonlocal games where each round can be not only won or lost by the players, but also discarded by the referee. Such games naturally formalize possibilistic proofs of nonlocality, such as Hardy's paradox. We develop algorithms for computing the local and Tsirelson bounds of post-selection games. Furthermore, we show that they have an unbounded advantage in statistical power over traditional nonlocal games, making them ideally suited for analysing Bell tests with low detection efficiency.

.
tldr: The paper introduces post-selection games, a generalization of nonlocal games with discarding outcomes, and develops methods to compute their local and Tsirelson bounds for Bell nonlocality analysis.
motivation: Standard nonlocal games do not naturally capture possibilistic nonlocality proofs such as Hardy's paradox or Bell tests with low detection efficiency, where some rounds are discarded.
method: The authors define post-selection games with win/lose/discard outcomes, develop algorithms for computing local and Tsirelson bounds, and analyze their statistical power compared with traditional nonlocal games.
result: Post-selection games can provide an unbounded statistical-power advantage over traditional nonlocal games and are well suited for analyzing Bell tests with low detection efficiency.
conclusion: Post-selection games offer a useful framework for possibilistic nonlocality proofs and detection-efficiency-limited Bell experiments, extending the theory of nonlocal games in a practically relevant direction.

title: Hardware-Efficient Entanglement Distillation Using Bosonic Systems
authors: Shoham Jacoby, Rotem Arnon-Friedman, And Serge Rosenblum
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2277 (2026).

High-fidelity entanglement shared between distant quantum systems is an essential resource for quantum communication and computation. Entanglement distillation addresses this need by converting multiple noisy Bell pairs into fewer higher-fidelity pairs, using only local quantum operations and classical communication. However, this approach typically requires a substantial overhead in the number of qubits. To bypass this hurdle, we propose to leverage the high-dimensional Hilbert space of a [MATH] pair of bosonic systems to store a large amount of entanglement, replacing the need for multi-qubit systems. To distill entanglement in such a setup, we devise a new entanglement distillation protocol, tailored for bosonic systems. The protocol converts a highly-entangled noisy state between two bosonic systems into a lower-dimensional but high-fidelity entangled state, using only local bosonic operations. We show that our protocol significantly enhances the fidelity of the entangled state in the presence of naturally occurring loss and dephasing errors. Compared to methods relying on multiple Bell pairs, our scheme offers a more hardware-efficient strategy, providing a practical route toward the realization of entanglement distillation.

.
tldr: The paper proposes a hardware-efficient entanglement distillation protocol that uses high-dimensional bosonic systems instead of multiple qubit pairs.
motivation: Entanglement distillation is essential for quantum communication and computation, but standard multi-qubit approaches incur large hardware overhead.
method: The authors design a distillation protocol tailored to a pair of bosonic systems, using local bosonic operations to convert a noisy highly entangled state into a lower-dimensional high-fidelity entangled state.
result: The protocol significantly improves entanglement fidelity under naturally occurring loss and dephasing errors while reducing the need for many qubits.
conclusion: Bosonic systems provide a practical and hardware-efficient route toward entanglement distillation for future quantum technologies.

title: Macroscopic Quantum Coherence And Entanglement In Mechanical Systems
authors: Benjamin Yadin And Matteo Fadel
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2257 (2026).

The notion of a macroscopic quantum state must be pinned down in order to assess how well experiments probe the large-scale limits of quantum mechanics. However, the issue of quantifying so-called quantum macroscopicity is fraught with multiple approaches having varying interpretations and levels of computability and measurability. Here, we introduce two measures that capture independent macroscopic properties: i) extensive size, measuring the degree of coherence in position or momentum observables relative to atomic-scale units, and ii) entangled size, quantifying the number of entangled subsystems. These measures unify many desirable features of past proposals while having rigorously justified interpretations from quantum information theory in terms of coherence and multipartite entanglement. We demonstrate how to estimate them and obtain lower-bounds using experimental data from micro-mechanical oscillators and diffracting molecules. Notably, we find evidence for genuine multipartite entanglement of [MATH] to [MATH] atoms in recent mechanical superposition states.

.
tldr: The paper introduces two quantum-information-theoretic measures of macroscopic quantum coherence and entanglement—extensive size and entangled size—and uses them to bound macroscopicity in mechanical superposition experiments.
motivation: Macroscopic quantum states require precise quantification to assess how experiments probe the large-scale limits of quantum mechanics, but existing macroscopicity measures vary in interpretation, computability, and measurability.
method: The authors define extensive size via coherence in position or momentum relative to atomic-scale units and entangled size via the number of entangled subsystems, then derive estimation and lower-bound techniques applicable to experimental data from micromechanical oscillators and diffracting molecules.
result: They find evidence for genuine multipartite entanglement of up to roughly 10^4–10^5 atoms in recent mechanical superposition states, using their rigorously justified coherence- and entanglement-based measures.
conclusion: The proposed measures unify desirable features of prior macroscopicity proposals while providing operational quantum-information interpretations and experimental lower bounds, clarifying how mechanical systems can exhibit macroscopic quantum coherence and entanglement.

title: Semi-device-independent Channel Identification With Communication Matrices
authors: Samgeeth Puliyil, Leevi Leppäjärvi, And Mário Ziman
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2274 (2026).

We look into the task of differentiating between any two quantum channels and reconstructing them from the obtained measurement statistics with possibly limited information about the experimental set-up. We employ the communication matrix formalism where the measurement statistics of a prepare-and-measure scenario is represented as a stochastic communication matrix. In order to differentiate between any two quantum channels, the informational completeness of the set-up is both necessary and sufficient. On the other hand, if we want to uniquely characterize any quantum channel, in addition we also need to have a complete description of the set-up. We show that in many important cases we can deduce this information directly from the communication matrix of the set-up before applying the channel. Given that we trust the dimension of the system, we show that we can deduce the information completeness of the set-up directly from the rank of the communication matrix. Furthermore, we show that another quantity of the communication matrix, called the information storability, can be used to self-test the set-up (up to an orthogonal transformation) for an important class of states and measurements. This provides us a semi-device-independent way to identify quantum channels from the prepare-and-measure statistics. Lastly, we consider scenarios where we might have some additional information about the channels or additional resources at our disposal which could help us relax some of the assumptions of the proposed scenario.

.
tldr: The paper develops a semi-device-independent framework using communication matrices to identify and self-test quantum channels from prepare-and-measure statistics.
motivation: Characterizing quantum channels typically requires strong assumptions about the experimental setup, so the authors aim to reduce these assumptions by extracting setup information directly from the observed prepare-and-measure statistics.
method: They represent measurement statistics as stochastic communication matrices and use informational completeness, matrix rank, and information storability to distinguish channels and self-test the setup up to orthogonal transformations.
result: The authors show that informational completeness is necessary and sufficient for channel discrimination, that rank can certify completeness given trusted dimension, and that information storability enables semi-device-independent self-testing for an important class of states and measurements.
conclusion: Communication-matrix methods provide a practical route to semi-device-independent channel identification and characterization, with possible relaxations when additional information or resources are available.

title: Variational Formulae For Entropy-like Functionals For States In Von Neumann Algebras
authors: Andrzej Łuczak, Hanna Podsędkowska, And Rafał Wieczorek
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2266 (2026).

The paper presents variational formulae for entropy-like functionals, including Segal and Rényi entropies, for normal states on semifinite von Neumann algebras. The considered functionals are of the form [MATH] where [MATH] is a normal faithful semifinite trace on this algebra, [MATH] is a positive selfadjoint operator from [MATH], and [MATH] is an appropriate convex or concave function. The results cover both finite and semifinite algebras, and the obtained formulae generalise known results, in particular, those concerning relative entropy. Moreover, the connection between quantum entropies and the structure of abelian subalgebras is highlighted, providing new interpretations in the context of quantum information theory.

.
tldr: The paper derives variational formulae for entropy-like functionals such as Segal and Rényi entropies for normal states on semifinite von Neumann algebras.
motivation: Entropy functionals are central to quantum information, but their variational characterizations in the general setting of von Neumann algebras remain important for extending information-theoretic tools beyond finite-dimensional systems.
method: The authors consider functionals defined via a normal faithful semifinite trace and a positive selfadjoint operator, using convex or concave functions to obtain variational expressions covering finite and semifinite algebras.
result: The formulae generalize known results, including those for relative entropy, and highlight connections between quantum entropies and the structure of abelian subalgebras.
conclusion: The work provides new mathematical tools and interpretations for quantum entropies in algebraic quantum information theory.

title: Quantum Authenticated Key Expansion With Key Recycling
authors: Wen Yu Kon, Jefferson Chu, Kevin Han Yong Loh, Obada Alia, Omar Amer, Marco Pistoia, Kaushik Chakraborty, And Charles Lim
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2255 (2026).

Data privacy and authentication are two main security requirements for remote access and cloud services. While QKD has been explored to address data privacy concerns, oftentimes its use is separate from the client authentication protocol despite implicitly providing authentication. Here, we present a quantum authentication key expansion (QAKE) protocol that (1) integrates both authentication and key expansion within a single protocol, and (2) provides key recycling property – allowing all authentication keys to be reused. We analyse the security of the protocol in a QAKE framework adapted from a classical authentication key exchange (AKE) framework, providing separate security conditions for authentication and data privacy. We experimentally implemented the protocol with appropriate post-selection. Additional results on the security of pseudorandom basis generation in QAKE and decoy state BB84 are provided.

.
tldr: The paper introduces a quantum authenticated key expansion protocol that combines authentication with key expansion and enables recycling of authentication keys.
motivation: Remote access and cloud services require both data privacy and authentication, but QKD is often treated separately from client authentication despite implicitly providing authentication.
method: The authors define a QAKE protocol and analyze its security within a QAKE framework adapted from classical authenticated key exchange, with separate conditions for authentication and data privacy; they also provide an experimental implementation with post-selection and analyses of pseudorandom basis generation in QAKE and decoy-state BB84.
result: The protocol integrates authentication and key expansion in a single quantum protocol while allowing all authentication keys to be reused, and the security analysis supports separate authentication and privacy guarantees.
conclusion: QAKE offers a practical quantum cryptographic approach that unifies authentication and key expansion with key recycling, supported by security analysis and experimental demonstration.

title: Certified Bounds On Optimization Problems In Quantum Theory
authors: Younes Naceur, Jie Wang, Victor Magron, And Antonio Acín
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2254 (2026).

Semidefinite relaxations of polynomial optimization have become a central tool for addressing the non-convex optimization problems over non-commutative operators that are ubiquitous in quantum information theory and, more in general, quantum physics. Yet, as these global relaxation methods are solved numerically, the bounds issued by the semidefinite solver can – and often do – exceed the global optimum, undermining their certifiability. To counter this issue, we introduce a framework for extracting rigorous certified bounds on non-commutative optimization problems from inexact numerical data, and apply it to several paradigmatic problems in quantum information theory. An extension to sparsity and symmetry-adapted semidefinite relaxations is also provided and compared to the general dense scheme. Our results establish rational post-processing as a practical route to reliable certification, pushing semidefinite optimization toward a certifiable standard for quantum information science.

.
tldr: The paper introduces a framework for extracting rigorously certified bounds from inexact numerical solutions of noncommutative polynomial optimization problems in quantum information theory.
motivation: Semidefinite relaxations are widely used to tackle non-convex operator optimization problems in quantum information, but numerical solver outputs can exceed the true global optimum, undermining their certifiability.
method: The authors develop rational post-processing techniques to convert inexact semidefinite solver data into rigorous certified bounds, with extensions to sparsity and symmetry-adapted relaxation schemes.
result: The framework is applied to several paradigmatic quantum information problems, demonstrating that rational post-processing can reliably certify bounds and comparing sparse/symmetry-adapted schemes with dense relaxations.
conclusion: The work establishes a practical route toward certifiable semidefinite optimization standards for quantum information science.

title: Towards Quantum Computing Feynman Diagrams In Hybrid Qubit-oscillator Devices
authors: S. Varona, S. Saner, O. Bäzävan, G. Araneda, G. Aarts, And A. Bermudez
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2252 (2026).

We show that recent experiments in hybrid qubit-oscillator devices that measure the phase-space characteristic function of the oscillator via the qubit can be seen through the lens of functional calculus and path integrals, drawing a clear analogy with the generating functional of a quantum field theory. This connection suggests an expansion of the characteristic function in terms of Feynman diagrams, exposing the role of the real-time bosonic propagator, and identifying the external source functions with certain time-dependent couplings that can be controlled experimentally. By applying maximum-likelihood techniques, we show that the “measurement'' of these Feynman diagrams can be reformulated as a problem of multi-parameter point estimation that takes as input a set of Ramsey-type measurements of the qubit. By numerical simulations that consider leading imperfections in trapped-ion devices, we identify the optimal regimes in which Feynman diagrams could be reconstructed from measured data with low systematic and stochastic errors. We discuss how these ideas can be generalized to finite temperatures via the Schwinger-Keldysh formalism, contributing to a bottom-up approach to probe quantum simulators of lattice field theories by systematically increasing the qubit-oscillator number.

.
tldr: The paper proposes reconstructing Feynman diagrams of a quantum field theory using phase-space characteristic-function measurements in hybrid qubit-oscillator devices.
motivation: Recent hybrid qubit-oscillator experiments can measure oscillator characteristic functions via the qubit, suggesting a connection between such measurements and functional/path-integral methods from quantum field theory.
method: The authors formulate the characteristic function as a generating functional, expand it in Feynman diagrams involving real-time bosonic propagators, and recast diagram measurement as multi-parameter point estimation from Ramsey-type qubit measurements using maximum-likelihood techniques.
result: Numerical simulations including leading trapped-ion imperfections identify regimes where Feynman diagrams can be reconstructed with low systematic and stochastic errors.
conclusion: The work provides a bottom-up route to probing quantum simulators of lattice field theories by increasing the number of hybrid qubit-oscillator components, with possible finite-temperature extensions via the Schwinger-Keldysh formalism.

title: Noncontextuality Inequalities For Prepare-transform-measure Scenarios
authors: David Schmid, Roberto D. Baldijão, John H. Selby, Ana Belén Sainz, And Robert W. Spekkens
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2250 (2026).

We provide the first systematic technique for deriving witnesses of contextuality in prepare-transform-measure scenarios. More specifically, we show how linear quantifier elimination can be used to compute a polytope of correlations consistent with generalized noncontextuality in such scenarios. This polytope is specified as a set of noncontextuality inequalities that are necessary and sufficient conditions for observed data in the scenario to admit of a classical explanation relative to any linear operational identities, if one ignores some constraints from diagram preservation. While including these latter constraints generally leads to tighter inequalities, it seems that nonlinear quantifier elimination would be required to systematically include them. We also provide a linear program which can certify the nonclassicality of a set of numerical data arising in a prepare-transform-measure experiment. We apply our results to get a robust noncontextuality inequality for transformations that can be violated within the stabilizer subtheory. Finally, we give a simple algorithm for computing all the linear operational identities holding among a given set of states, of transformations, or of measurements.

.
tldr: The paper introduces a systematic method for deriving noncontextuality inequalities in prepare-transform-measure scenarios using linear quantifier elimination and applies it to certify nonclassicality.
motivation: Contextuality witnesses in prepare-transform-measure scenarios are important for foundational tests and operational nonclassicality, but systematic derivation methods have been lacking.
method: The authors compute a polytope of correlations consistent with generalized noncontextuality via linear quantifier elimination, formulate a linear program for certifying nonclassical data, and give an algorithm for finding linear operational identities.
result: They obtain noncontextuality inequalities that are necessary and sufficient under linear operational identities, derive a robust inequality for transformations violated in the stabilizer subtheory, and provide a practical certification linear program.
conclusion: This provides the first systematic framework for deriving prepare-transform-measure noncontextuality inequalities, with applications to robust nonclassicality certification and potential extensions requiring nonlinear quantifier elimination.

title: Distinguishability Of Locally Diagonal Orthogonally Invariant Quantum States
authors: Nathaniel Johnston And Vincent Russo
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2275 (2026).

We study the distinguishability of quantum states under local operations with classical communication (LOCC), separable, and positive-partial-transpose (PPT) measurements, focusing on locally diagonal orthogonally invariant (LDOI) states – those invariant under local diagonal orthogonal twirling. This class includes many important families such as Werner states, isotropic states, X-states, and Dicke states. We show that optimal PPT and separable measurements for distinguishing LDOI states can always be taken to be LDOI, and the LOCC supremum can be approached by LDOI LOCC POVMs, enabling a dimensional reduction from [MATH] to [MATH] in the associated optimization problems. We establish efficiently computable bounds on the distinguishability of orthonormal LDOI bases and prove that for a broad class of such bases – including all two-qubit cases – the LOCC supremum equals the PPT and separable optima. More generally, we show the gap between PPT and LOCC distinguishability is at most [MATH] for local dimension [MATH].

.
tldr: The paper studies distinguishability of locally diagonal orthogonally invariant (LDOI) quantum states under LOCC, separable, and PPT measurements, showing that optimal measurements can be chosen within the LDOI class and deriving bounds on the LOCC-versus-PPT gap.
motivation: Restricted measurement classes such as LOCC and PPT are operationally important but generally hard to optimize, and LDOI states include many common families like Werner, isotropic, X, and Dicke states.
method: The authors exploit local diagonal orthogonal invariance and twirling to restrict optimal PPT and separable measurements to LDOI form, reduce the optimization dimension, and derive efficiently computable bounds on distinguishability for orthonormal LDOI bases.
result: For a broad class of LDOI bases, including all two-qubit cases, the LOCC supremum equals the PPT and separable optima, and more generally the PPT-LOCC distinguishability gap is bounded by a small dimension-dependent quantity.
conclusion: Symmetry under local diagonal orthogonal twirling substantially simplifies restricted state discrimination and clarifies when LOCC, separable, and PPT measurements perform equivalently.

title: Learning State Preparation Circuits For Quantum Phases Of Matter
authors: Hyun-Soo Kim, Isaac H. Kim, And Daniel Ranard
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2270 (2026).

Many-body ground state preparation is an important subroutine used in the simulation of physical systems. In this paper, we introduce a flexible and efficient framework for obtaining a state preparation circuit for a large class of many-body ground states. We introduce polynomial-time classical algorithms that take reduced density matrices over [MATH]-sized balls as inputs, and output a circuit that prepares the global state. We introduce algorithms applicable to (i) short-range entangled states (e.g., states prepared by shallow quantum circuits in any number of dimensions, and more generally, invertible states) and (ii) long-range entangled ground states (e.g., the toric code on a disk). Both algorithms can provably find a circuit whose depth is asymptotically optimal. Our approach uses a variant of the quantum Markov chain condition that remains robust against constant-depth circuits. The robustness of this condition makes our method applicable to a large class of states, whilst ensuring a classically tractable optimization landscape.

.
tldr: The paper introduces classical algorithms that use local reduced density matrices to construct asymptotically optimal-depth circuits for preparing many-body ground states, including short-range entangled and topological states.
motivation: Many-body ground state preparation is an important subroutine for quantum simulation, but systematically obtaining efficient preparation circuits for broad classes of states remains challenging.
method: The authors develop polynomial-time algorithms based on a robust variant of the quantum Markov chain condition, taking reduced density matrices on small balls as input and outputting state preparation circuits.
result: The framework applies to short-range entangled states, invertible states, and long-range entangled ground states such as the toric code on a disk, and provably finds circuits with asymptotically optimal depth.
conclusion: The robustness of the quantum Markov chain condition against constant-depth circuits yields a tractable and broadly applicable method for learning state preparation circuits for quantum phases of matter.

title: Sequential Realization Of Quantum Instruments
authors: Soham Sau And Michal Sedlák
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2262 (2026).

In adaptive quantum circuits classical results of mid-circuit measurements determine the upcoming gates. This allows POVMs, quantum channels or more generally quantum instruments to be implemented sequentially, so that fewer qubits need to be used at each of the [MATH] measurement steps. In this paper, we mathematically describe these problems via adaptive sequence of instruments (ASI) and show how any instrument can be decomposed into it. Number of steps [MATH] and number of ancillary qubits [MATH] needed for actual implementation are crucial parameters of any such ASI. We show an achievable lower bound on the product [MATH] and we determine in which situations this tradeoff is likely to be optimal. Contrary to common intuition we show that for quantum instruments which transform [MATH] to [MATH] qubits, there exist [MATH]-step ASI implementing them just with [MATH] ancillary qubits, which are remeasured [MATH] times and finally used as output qubits.

.
tldr: The paper formalizes adaptive sequences of quantum instruments and derives resource tradeoffs for sequentially implementing general quantum instruments with fewer ancillary qubits.
motivation: Adaptive quantum circuits with classical feedforward from mid-circuit measurements can implement POVMs, channels, and general quantum instruments sequentially, reducing the number of qubits needed at each measurement step.
method: The authors introduce adaptive sequences of instruments (ASI), show that any quantum instrument can be decomposed into such a sequence, and analyze the tradeoff between the number of steps and the number of ancillary qubits.
result: They obtain an achievable lower bound on the product of the number of steps and ancillary qubits, characterize when this tradeoff is likely optimal, and show that certain instruments can be implemented with surprisingly few ancillary qubits that are repeatedly remeasured and then used as output qubits.
conclusion: The ASI framework provides a systematic way to understand and optimize resource costs in the sequential implementation of quantum instruments using adaptive measurement-based circuits.

title: Lower-depth Local Encoding Circuits For The Surface Code
authors: Jahan Claes
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2267 (2026).

The surface code is the most studied error-correcting code thanks to its high threshold, simple decoding, and locality in two dimensions (2D). A key component of any code is its encoding circuit, which maps an unencoded state to the corresponding encoded state. The best previous surface code encoding circuit compatible with 2D local connectivity requires depth [MATH] to encode distance-[MATH] surface codes. This paper presents depth [MATH] encoding circuits for the rotated surface code. Our circuit is constructed inductively from circuits that grow the code from [MATH] to [MATH]. We prove that depth [MATH] is optimal for inductively constructed circuits.

.
tldr: This paper constructs lower-depth local encoding circuits for the rotated surface code, achieving depth O(sqrt(n)) and proving optimality within an inductive construction.
motivation: Encoding circuits are essential for initializing error-correcting codes, but surface-code encodings compatible with 2D local connectivity previously required circuit depth O(n).
method: The authors inductively build encoding circuits that grow a distance-d surface code from distance-(d-1) codes, using locality constraints in two dimensions.
result: They obtain depth O(sqrt(n)) encoding circuits for the rotated surface code and prove that this depth is optimal for inductively constructed circuits.
conclusion: The work improves surface-code initialization overhead and clarifies depth limitations for locally connected inductive encoding schemes.

title: Rotating-Wave And Secular Approximations For Open Quantum Systems
authors: Daniel Burgarth, Paolo Facchi, Giovanni Gramegna, And Kazuya Yuasa
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2264 (2026).

We derive a nonperturbative bound on the distance between evolutions of open quantum systems described by time-dependent generators. We show how this result can be employed to provide an explicit upper bound on the error of the rotating-wave approximation in the presence of dissipation and decoherence. We apply the derived bound to the strong-coupling limit in open quantum systems and to the secular approximation used to obtain a master equation of the Gorini-Kossakowski-Lindblad-Sudarshan form from the Redfield master equation.

.
tldr: The authors derive a nonperturbative bound on the distance between evolutions of open quantum systems with time-dependent generators, and use it to rigorously bound errors of the rotating-wave and secular approximations in the presence of dissipation and decoherence.
motivation: Rotating-wave and secular approximations are ubiquitous in deriving GKSL master equations from Redfield theory, yet their validity in the presence of dissipation and strong coupling is often justified only heuristically; a quantitative, nonperturbative error bound is needed.
method: A general distance bound between propagators of time-dependent generators is proven, then specialized to quantify the error of the rotating-wave approximation and of the secular approximation that reduces the Redfield equation to GKSL form.
result: Explicit upper bounds on the approximation error are obtained, including in the strong-coupling regime, providing conditions under which the approximated master equations faithfully reproduce the true open-system dynamics.
conclusion: The framework puts commonly used Markovian approximations in open quantum system theory on rigorous quantitative footing, clarifying regimes of validity and offering a practical error-control tool.

title: QwaveMPS: An Efficient Open-source Python Package For Simulating non-Markovian waveguide-QED Using Matrix Product States
authors: Sofia Arranz Regidor, Matthew Kozma, And Stephen Hughes
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2258 (2026).

QwaveMPS is an open-source Python library for simulating one-dimensional quantum many-body waveguide systems using matrix product states (MPS). It provides a user-friendly interface for constructing, evolving, and analyzing quantum states and operators, facilitating studies in quantum physics and quantum information with waveguide-QED systems. This approach enables efficient, scalable simulations by focusing computational resources on the most relevant parts of the quantum system. Thus, one can study a wide range of complex dynamical interactions, including time-delayed feedback effects in the non-Markovian regime and deeply nonlinear systems, at a highly reduced computational cost compared to full Hilbert space approaches, making it both practical and convenient to model a variety of open waveguide-QED systems (in Markovian and non-Markovian regimes), treating quantized atoms and quantized photons on an equal footing. The QwaveMPS package automates the waveguide-QED-specific tensor-network operations, including construction of the time-bin evolution operator from physical parameters, the swap network required for delayed interactions, orthogonality-center and truncation management, the matrix-product factorization of [MATH]-photon Fock-state inputs, and the evaluation of single-time and two-time field observables (such as the second-order quantum correlation function) at chosen points along the waveguide.

The code is available at GitHub.

.
tldr: QwaveMPS is an open-source Python package for efficient matrix-product-state simulation of non-Markovian waveguide-QED systems.
motivation: Simulating one-dimensional quantum many-body waveguide systems with time-delayed feedback and strong nonlinearities is computationally challenging using full Hilbert-space methods.
method: The package automates waveguide-QED-specific tensor-network operations, including time-bin evolution operators, swap networks for delayed interactions, truncation management, Fock-state matrix-product factorization, and field-observable evaluation.
result: It enables scalable modeling of quantized atoms and photons on equal footing in both Markovian and non-Markovian regimes at reduced computational cost.
conclusion: QwaveMPS provides a practical simulation tool for open waveguide-QED systems, though its contribution is primarily computational rather than a new information-theoretic or thermodynamic result.

title: A Counterexample To The Optimality Conjecture In Convex Quantum Channel Optimization
authors: Jianting Yang
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2253 (2026).

This paper presents a counterexample to the optimality conjecture for the trace distance based optimal state transformation problem proposed by Coutts et al. [Quantum 5, 448 (2021)]. The conjecture posits that for the trace distance based optimal state transformation problem, applying the sign function to the error matrix uniquely determines a dual certificate for every optimal solution. By constructing a counterexample in 2-dimensional Hilbert spaces, we disprove this conjecture.

.
tldr: The paper constructs an explicit two-dimensional counterexample disproving the conjecture that the sign function of the error matrix always yields a dual certificate for trace-distance-based optimal state transformation problems.
motivation: Coutts et al. (Quantum 5, 448) conjectured that for the trace-distance-based optimal state transformation problem, applying the sign function to the error matrix uniquely determines a dual certificate for every optimal solution; verifying or refuting such structural conjectures is essential for trusting the associated numerical and analytical methods.
method: The author builds an explicit counterexample within 2-dimensional Hilbert spaces, exhibiting an optimal state transformation whose error matrix's sign function fails to serve as a valid dual certificate.
result: The conjecture is false: a concrete low-dimensional instance is given in which the proposed sign-function construction does not produce a dual certificate for the optimal solution.
conclusion: The optimality conjecture of Coutts et al. must be abandoned or amended; the counterexample clarifies the limits of the sign-function certificate construction and motivates more careful certification criteria in convex quantum channel optimization.

title: Optimal Phase Estimation In The Presence Of Correlated Dephasing
authors: Srijon Ghosh, Arkadiusz Kobus, Stanisław Kurdziałek, And Rafał Demkowicz-Dobrzański
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2251 (2026).

We investigate optimal metrological protocols for phase estimation in the presence of correlated dephasing noise, including spin-squeezed state sensing strategies as well as parallel and adaptive protocols optimized using tensor-network-based numerical methods. The results are benchmarked against fundamental bounds obtained either via the latest quantum comb extension method or an optimized classical simulation method. We find that the spin-squeezed states offer practically optimal performance in the regime where phase fluctuations are positively correlated but can be outperformed by tensor-network-optimized strategies for negatively correlated fluctuations.

.
tldr: The paper determines optimal phase-estimation protocols under correlated dephasing noise, comparing spin-squeezed strategies with tensor-network-optimized parallel and adaptive schemes against fundamental bounds from quantum comb extension and optimized classical simulation.
motivation: Correlated dephasing noise is a dominant obstacle in realistic quantum metrology, and it is unclear which sensing strategies (spin squeezing versus numerically optimized adaptive protocols) remain optimal when noise correlations are positive or negative.
method: The authors benchmark spin-squeezed-state sensing, parallel protocols, and adaptive protocols optimized via tensor networks against fundamental precision bounds derived from the quantum comb extension method and an optimized classical simulation approach.
result: Spin-squeezed states are found to be practically optimal for positively correlated phase fluctuations, while tensor-network-optimized strategies outperform them when fluctuations are negatively correlated.
conclusion: The choice of optimal metrological strategy depends qualitatively on the sign of noise correlations, and numerical tensor-network optimization combined with fundamental bounds provides a practical guide for designing robust phase-estimation protocols.

title: Symmetries, Correlation Functions, And Entanglement Of General Quantum Motzkin Spin-chains
authors: Varun Menon, Andi Gu, And Ramis Movassagh
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2279 (2026).

Motzkin spin-chains, which include `colorless' (integer spin [MATH]) and `colorful' ([MATH]) variants, are one-dimensional (1D) local integer spin models notable for their lack of a conformal field theory (CFT) description of their low-energy physics, despite being gapless. The colorful variants are particularly unusual, as they exhibit power-law violation of the area-law of entanglement entropy (as [MATH] in system size [MATH]), rather than a logarithmic violation as seen in a CFT. In this work, we analytically discover several unique properties of these models, potentially suggesting a new universality class for their low-energy physics. We identify a complex structure of symmetries and unexpected scaling behavior in spin-spin correlations, which deviate from known 1D universality classes. Specifically, the [MATH] chain exhibits [MATH] spontaneous symmetry breaking and ferromagnetic order. Meanwhile, the [MATH] chains do not appear to spontaneously break any symmetries, but display quasi-long-range algebraic order with power-law decaying correlations, inconsistent with standard Berezinskii-Kosterlitz-Thouless (BKT) critical exponents. We also derive asymptotic scaling expressions, with explicit additive constants, for entanglement measures in both colorless and colorful chains, generalizing previous results of Movassagh [5], while providing benchmarks for potential quantum simulation experiments. The [MATH] entanglement scaling implies that any matrix-product-state description of these ground states requires bond dimension [MATH]; this superpolynomial cost of the standard 1D tensor-network toolkit, along with the analytical tractability of their ground state properties, positions Motzkin spin chains as intriguing testbeds for quantum simulation of many-body physics.

.
tldr: Analytical study of Motzkin spin chains uncovers unusual symmetries, correlation scaling, and entanglement entropy scaling that suggest a new universality class and challenge standard tensor-network descriptions.
motivation: Motzkin spin chains are gapless 1D models without a CFT description, and colorful variants exhibit power-law violation of the entanglement area law, making their low-energy and entanglement structure interesting but not directly aligned with core quantum information protocols.
method: The authors analytically derive symmetry structures, spin-spin correlation functions, and asymptotic entanglement scaling expressions with explicit additive constants for colorless and colorful Motzkin chains.
result: The integer-spin chain shows spontaneous symmetry breaking and ferromagnetic order, while colorful chains display quasi-long-range algebraic order with non-BKT exponents; entanglement scaling implies superpolynomial matrix-product-state bond dimension.
conclusion: Motzkin spin chains provide analytically tractable testbeds for quantum simulation of many-body physics and highlight limitations of standard 1D tensor-network methods.

title: Quantum Channel Testing In Average-Case Distance
authors: Gregory Rosenthal, Hugo Aaronson, Sathyawageeswar Subramanian, Animesh Datta, And Tom Gur
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2276 (2026).

We study the complexity of testing properties of quantum channels. First, we show that testing identity to any channel [MATH] in diamond norm distance requires [MATH] queries, even in the strongest algorithmic model that admits ancillae, coherence, and adaptivity. This is due to the worst-case nature of the distance induced by the diamond norm. Motivated by this limitation and other theoretical and practical applications, we introduce an average-case analogue of the diamond norm, which we call the average-case imitation diamond (ACID) norm. In the weakest algorithmic model without ancillae, coherence, or adaptivity, we prove that testing identity to certain types of channels in ACID distance can be done with complexity independent of the dimensions of the channel, while for other types of channels the complexity depends on both the input and output dimensions. Building on previous work, we also show that identity to any fixed channel can be tested with [MATH] queries in ACID distance and [MATH] queries in diamond distance in this model. Finally, we prove tight bounds on the complexity of channel tomography in ACID distance.

.
tldr: The paper studies the query complexity of testing properties of quantum channels, showing diamond-norm identity testing is inherently hard and introducing an average-case analogue (the ACID norm) that permits dimension-independent testing in restricted models.
motivation: Diamond-norm distance is worst-case and thus forces query complexity to scale with channel dimension, motivating both a lower-bound analysis and a more practical average-case distance measure for channel certification.
method: Proves query lower bounds for identity testing in diamond norm across the strongest (ancilla-assisted, adaptive, coherent) algorithmic models, then defines the average-case imitation diamond (ACID) norm and analyzes testing and tomography complexity under it in weaker models without ancillae or adaptivity.
result: Identity testing in diamond norm requires dimension-dependent queries regardless of model, whereas in ACID distance some channel classes can be tested with dimension-independent complexity (others depend on input/output dimensions); tight bounds on ACID-distance channel tomography are also established.
conclusion: Average-case channel distance measures offer a viable route to efficient channel certification where worst-case diamond-norm testing is provably intractable, sharpening the complexity landscape of quantum channel testing.

title: Simulating Gaussian Boson Sampling On Graphs In Polynomial Time
authors: Konrad Anand, Zongchen Chen, Mary Cryan, Graham Freifeld, Leslie Ann Goldberg, Heng Guo, And Xinyuan Zhang
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2268 (2026).

We show that a distribution related to Gaussian Boson Sampling (GBS) on graphs can be sampled classically in polynomial time. Graphical applications of GBS typically sample from this distribution, and thus quantum algorithms do not provide exponential speedup for these applications. We also show that another distribution related to Boson sampling can be sampled classically in polynomial time.

.
tldr: The paper gives polynomial-time classical algorithms for sampling distributions related to Gaussian Boson Sampling on graphs, showing no exponential quantum speedup for these specific graphical applications.
motivation: Gaussian Boson Sampling and Boson Sampling are often proposed as routes to quantum computational advantage, so identifying structured settings where classical simulation is efficient is important for delimiting that advantage.
method: The authors construct classical polynomial-time sampling algorithms for a GBS-related distribution on graphs and for another Boson-sampling-related distribution, exploiting the graph-structured nature of these computational problems.
result: They prove that the relevant graph-based GBS distribution and another Boson-sampling-related distribution can be sampled classically in polynomial time, implying that these particular applications do not enjoy an exponential quantum speedup.
conclusion: The work clarifies the limitations of graphical GBS/Boson-sampling applications as demonstrations of quantum advantage, though it does not rule out quantum advantage in more general Boson-sampling settings.

title: Cryptanalysis Of Isogeny-Based Quantum Money With Rational Points
authors: Hyeonhak Kim, Donghoe Heo, Seokhie Hong, Sangjin Lee, And Suhri Kim
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2263 (2026).

Quantum money is a representative application in cryptography that utilizes quantum technology to achieve security that is unattainable with classical systems. Since the theoretical proposal by Wiesner in 1983, the most recent instantiation is the quantum money using class group actions on elliptic curves, proposed by Montgomery and Sharif in Asiacrypt'24. In this work, we propose a concrete cryptanalysis by leveraging the efficiency of evaluating division polynomials with the coordinates of rational points, offering a speedup of [MATH] compared to the brute-force attack. While the resulting attack still runs in exponential time, our method provides the first nontrivial algorithmic insight into their structural hardness. Furthermore, due to the algebraic properties of rational points and quadratic twists, our technique naturally yields a more efficient verification procedure for the underlying quantum money. We believe this new line of analysis opens promising directions for future research in elliptic-curve-based quantum cryptography.

.
tldr: The paper presents a cryptanalytic attack on an isogeny-based quantum money scheme by exploiting efficient evaluation of division polynomials at rational points.
motivation: Quantum money based on class group actions on elliptic curves is a recent cryptographic proposal, and its structural hardness had not yet received nontrivial algorithmic analysis.
method: The authors use algebraic properties of rational points and quadratic twists to evaluate division polynomials efficiently, yielding a speedup over brute-force attacks and a more efficient verification procedure.
result: The attack remains exponential but provides the first nontrivial algorithmic insight into the scheme's hardness, along with an improved verification method.
conclusion: The work opens a new line of analysis for elliptic-curve-based quantum cryptography, though it does not break the scheme.

title: Computational Complexity Of Berry Phase Estimation In Topological Phases Of Matter
authors: Ryu Hayakawa, Kazuki Sakamoto, And Chusei Kiumi
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2271 (2026).

The Berry phase is a fundamental quantity in the classification of topological phases of matter. In this paper, we present a new quantum algorithm and several complexity-theoretical results for the Berry phase estimation (BPE) problems. Our new quantum algorithm achieves BPE in a more general setting than previously known quantum algorithms, with a theoretical guarantee. For the complexity-theoretic results, we consider two main cases. First, we prove [MATH]-completeness when we are given a guiding state that has a large overlap with the ground state. This result establishes an exponential quantum speedup for estimating the Berry phase. Second, we prove [MATH]-[MATH]-completeness when we have an [MATH] bound for the ground-state energy. Here, [MATH] is the unique witness version of [MATH], and [MATH]-[MATH] precisely captures the complexity of BPE without the known guiding state. Remarkably, this problem is, to our knowledge, the first natural problem complete for [MATH]-[MATH]. These results advance the role of quantum computing in the study of topological phases of matter and provide a pathway for clarifying the connection between topological phases of matter and computational complexity.

.
tldr: The paper develops quantum algorithms and complexity-theoretic classifications for estimating Berry phases in topological phases of matter.
motivation: Berry phase is central to topological classification, and the authors aim to clarify its computational complexity and quantum speedup potential.
method: They introduce a new quantum algorithm for Berry phase estimation and prove completeness results for complexity classes under guiding-state and energy-bound assumptions.
result: They establish QMA-completeness with a guiding state, implying exponential quantum speedup, and prove QMA-UNIQUE-completeness under a ground-state energy bound, identifying the first natural problem in that class.
conclusion: The work connects topological phases to computational complexity and advances quantum algorithms for Berry phase estimation, but is primarily a complexity-theory contribution.

title: Re-uploading Quantum Data: A Universal Function Approximator For Quantum Inputs
authors: Hyunho Cha, Daniel K. Park, And Jungwoo Lee
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2256 (2026).

Quantum data re-uploading has proved powerful for classical inputs, where repeatedly encoding features into a small circuit yields universal function approximation. Extending this idea to quantum inputs remains underexplored, as the information contained in a quantum state is not directly accessible in classical form. We propose and analyze a quantum data re-uploading architecture in which a qubit interacts sequentially with fresh copies of an arbitrary input state. The circuit can approximate any bounded continuous function using only one ancilla qubit and single-qubit measurements, provided that sufficiently many copies of the input state and, in general, sufficiently many layers are available. By alternating entangling unitaries with mid-circuit resets of the input register, the architecture realizes a discrete cascade of completely positive and trace-preserving maps, analogous to collision models in open quantum system dynamics. Our framework provides a space-efficient and expressive approach to designing quantum machine learning models that operate directly on quantum data.

.
tldr: The paper proposes a quantum data re-uploading architecture that processes quantum inputs by sequentially interacting a qubit with fresh copies of an input state, enabling universal approximation of bounded continuous functions.
motivation: Data re-uploading is well established for classical inputs, but its extension to quantum inputs is underexplored because quantum information cannot be directly accessed classically.
method: A small quantum circuit repeatedly couples an ancilla qubit to copies of an arbitrary input state, alternating entangling unitaries with mid-circuit resets of the input register to realize a discrete cascade of completely positive trace-preserving maps.
result: The architecture can approximate any bounded continuous function using one ancilla qubit and single-qubit measurements, given sufficiently many input copies and layers.
conclusion: The work offers a space-efficient and expressive framework for quantum machine learning directly on quantum data, analogous to collision models in open quantum systems.

The work here enables a cost scaling of [MATH] and maximum depth [MATH] for estimating observables after some Hamiltonian evolution [MATH] using no extra block-encoding qubits, where [MATH] is the algorithmic error of the target Hamiltonian evolution and [MATH] is the statistical error from the observable estimation. Throughout, [MATH] suppresses factors that are doubly logarithmic in [MATH] (i.e. [MATH]), which are subdominant to the displayed [MATH] factors. motivation: Hamiltonian simulation and observable estimation are central quantum-algorithmic tasks, and improved cost/depth scaling with fewer ancillary qubits is desirable for near-term and fault-tolerant implementations.
method: The approach combines product formulas with stable Chebyshev interpolation for Hamiltonian evolution and cardinal sine interpolation for fractional queries, using an optimized variable-order product formula.

title: Improved Parameter Initialization For The (local) Unitary Cluster Jastrow Ansatz
authors: Wan-Hsuan Lin, Fangchun Liang, Mario Motta, Haimeng Zhang, Kenneth M. Merz Jr., And Kevin J. Sung
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2278 (2026).

The unitary cluster Jastrow (UCJ) ansatz and its variant known as local UCJ (LUCJ) are promising choices for variational quantum algorithms for chemistry due to their combination of physical motivation and hardware efficiency. The parameters of these ansatzes can be initialized from the output of a coupled cluster, singles and doubles (CCSD) calculation performed on a classical computer. However, truncating the number of repetitions of the ansatz, as well as discarding interactions to accommodate the connectivity constraints of near-term quantum processors, degrade the approximation to CCSD and the resulting energy accuracy. In this work, we propose two methods to improve the parameter initialization. The first method, which is applicable to both expectation value- and sample-based algorithms, uses compressed double factorization of the CCSD amplitudes to improve or recover the CCSD approximation. The second method, which is applicable to sample-based algorithms, uses approximate tensor network simulation to improve the quality of samples produced by the ansatz circuit. Both methods perform classical preprocessing to construct the initial circuit parameters and can be followed by parameter optimization using quantum measurements, although we do not perform such optimization in this work. We validate our methods using exact state vector simulation on systems of up to 52 qubits, as well as experiments on superconducting quantum processors using up to 65 qubits. Our results indicate that our methods can significantly improve the output of both expectation value- and sample-based quantum algorithms.

.
tldr: The authors propose two classical-preprocessing methods to improve parameter initialization for the unitary cluster Jastrow (UCJ) and local UCJ ansatzes used in variational quantum algorithms for quantum chemistry.
motivation: Truncating ansatz repetitions and discarding interactions to satisfy hardware connectivity degrades the CCSD-derived initialization of UCJ/LUCJ circuits, reducing achievable energy accuracy on near-term devices.
method: One method uses compressed double factorization of CCSD amplitudes to recover the CCSD approximation for both expectation-value- and sample-based algorithms; the other uses approximate tensor-network simulation to improve sample quality for sample-based algorithms.
result: Validation via exact state-vector simulation up to 52 qubits and experiments on superconducting processors up to 65 qubits shows the initialization methods significantly improve the output of both expectation-value- and sample-based algorithms.
conclusion: Classical preprocessing of UCJ/LUCJ initial parameters can substantially mitigate hardware-connectivity-induced accuracy loss, though quantum-measurement-based parameter optimization is left to future work.

title: Below-shot-noise Capacity In Phase Estimation Using Nonlinear Interferometers
authors: Cristofero Oglialoro, Gerard J. Machado, Felix Farsch, Daniel F. Urrego, Alejandra A. Padilla, Raj B. Patel, Ian A. Walmsley, Markus Gräfe, Juan P. Torres, And Enno Giese
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2272 (2026).

Over the past decade, several schemes for imaging and sensing based on nonlinear interferometers have been proposed and demonstrated experimentally. These interferometers exhibit two main advantages. First, they enable probing a sample at a chosen wavelength while detecting light at a different wavelength with high efficiency (bicolor quantum imaging and sensing with undetected light). Second, they can show quantum-enhanced sensitivities below the shot-noise limit, potentially reaching Heisenberg-limited precision in parameter estimation. Here, we compare three quantum-imaging configurations using only easily accessible intensity-based measurements for phase estimation: a Yurke-type SU(1,1) interferometer, a Mandel-type induced-coherence interferometer, and a hybrid scheme that continuously interpolates between them. While an ideal Yurke interferometer can exhibit Heisenberg scaling, this advantage is known to be fragile under realistic detection constraints and in the presence of loss. We demonstrate that differential intensity detection in the Mandel interferometer provides the highest and most robust phase sensitivity among the considered schemes, reaching but not surpassing the shot-noise limit, even in the presence of loss. Intensity measurements in a Yurke-type configuration can achieve genuine sub-shot-noise sensitivity under balanced losses and moderate gain; however, their performance degrades in realistic high-gain regimes. Consequently, in this regime, the Mandel configuration with differential detection outperforms the Yurke-type setup and constitutes the most robust approach for phase estimation.

.
tldr: The paper compares three nonlinear interferometer configurations for phase estimation using intensity measurements, finding that Mandel-type differential detection is the most robust but does not surpass the shot-noise limit, while Yurke-type setups can achieve sub-shot-noise sensitivity only under restrictive loss and gain conditions.
motivation: Nonlinear interferometers are attractive for bicolor quantum imaging and sensing with undetected light and can in principle provide quantum-enhanced sensitivity, but their practical advantage under realistic detection and loss is unclear.
method: The authors theoretically analyze and compare a Yurke-type SU(1,1) interferometer, a Mandel-type induced-coherence interferometer, and a hybrid scheme using easily accessible intensity-based measurements for phase estimation, including the effects of loss.
result: Differential intensity detection in the Mandel interferometer gives the highest and most robust phase sensitivity, reaching but not surpassing the shot-noise limit even with loss; Yurke-type intensity measurements can show genuine sub-shot-noise sensitivity under balanced losses and moderate gain but degrade at realistic high gain.
conclusion: For realistic high-gain regimes with loss, the Mandel configuration with differential detection is the most robust approach, while the Heisenberg-like advantage of the ideal Yurke interferometer is fragile under practical constraints.

title: Fast Simulations Of X-ray Absorption Spectroscopy For Battery Materials On A Quantum Computer
authors: Stepan Fomichev, Pablo A. M. Casares, Jay Soni, Utkarsh Azad, Alexander Kunitsa, Arne-Christian Voigt, Jonathan E. Mueller, And Juan Miguel Arrazola
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2265 (2026).

X-ray absorption spectroscopy (XAS) is a leading technique for understanding structural changes in advanced battery materials such as lithium-excess cathodes. However, extracting critical information like oxidation states from the experimental spectra requires expensive and time-consuming simulations. Building upon a recent proposal to simulate XAS using quantum computers, this work proposes a highly-optimized implementation of the time-domain algorithm for X-ray absorption. Among a host of improvements to Hamiltonian representation, circuit implementation, and measurement strategies, three optimizations are key to the efficiency of the algorithm. The first is the use of product formulas with the compressed double factorized form of the Hamiltonian. The second is recognizing that for spectroscopy applications, it is sufficient to control the error in the eigenvalues of the (approximate) Hamiltonian being implemented by the product formula, rather than the generic error on the full time evolution operator. Using perturbation theory to estimate this eigenvalue error, we find that significantly fewer Trotter steps are needed than expected from the time evolution error bound. The third is the choice of an optimized distribution of samples that takes advantage of the exponentially decaying Lorentzian kernel. Through constant factor resource estimates, we show that a challenging model Li[MATH]Mn[MATH]O cluster system with 18 spatial orbitals and 22 electrons in the active space can be simulated with 100 logical qubits and less than [MATH] Toffoli gates per circuit. Finally, the algorithm is implemented on a simulator, and the reconstructed spectrum is verified against a classical computational reference. The low cost of our algorithm makes it attractive to use on fault-tolerant quantum devices to accelerate the development and commercialization of high-capacity battery cathodes.

.
tldr: The paper develops an optimized time-domain quantum algorithm for simulating X-ray absorption spectra of battery materials, with resource estimates for a LiMn2O4-type cluster and simulator validation.
motivation: X-ray absorption spectroscopy is important for understanding battery cathode materials, but extracting oxidation-state information requires expensive classical simulations; quantum computers may accelerate these simulations.
method: The authors optimize a time-domain XAS simulation algorithm using compressed double-factorized Hamiltonians, product formulas, eigenvalue-error-based Trotter step estimates, and an optimized sampling distribution for the Lorentzian kernel.
result: They estimate that an 18-orbital, 22-electron active-space cluster can be simulated with 100 logical qubits and fewer than a specified number of Toffoli gates per circuit, and they verify the reconstructed spectrum against a classical reference on a simulator.
conclusion: The low resource cost makes the algorithm attractive for fault-tolerant quantum devices and potentially useful for accelerating battery materials development, though it is primarily a quantum-chemistry simulation application.
